title: Snapshots, forks and templates
standfirst: Four jobs hide under “snapshot”: a restore point on one machine, a reusable image for new machines, a copy of a running machine, and a backup that survives losing the host. Ask which one you are getting.
idea: A restore point lets you rewind one machine after a bad change. A reusable image lets you start many identical machines from a known-good setup. A fork copies a machine, ideally while it is running, so you can try something without risking the original. A backup survives losing the host or the account.

Memory is the dividing line. A snapshot with memory can resume a half-finished agent turn; a disk-only snapshot cannot. Fork is the same split: a disk fork boots cold, a memory fork resumes mid-task. A “live” fork may still pause the source for a moment, and several providers do exactly that.

Templates are the third axis. They can be a Docker image, a named snapshot, or a fixed catalogue entry. That decides whether you can carry your own setup forward or are choosing from what the provider built.

splits.heading: A snapshot with memory is not a backup
body: E2B, Morph, Lizard, boxd, Blaxel and Runtime all capture memory and processes in at least one snapshot mode. That makes them useful for cloning a working agent. It does not make them disaster recovery: a copy on the same host or cluster can disappear with it.

Boat's snapshots are automatic, disk-only and taken every minute, but only the newest is usable. Agent 37 has no snapshot product at all: a sleep checkpoint that cannot be cloned, a folder backup, and Dockerfile templates.

splits.heading: Fork is not always live
body: boxd forks memory and disk in 100–200 ms while the source pauses for a fraction of a second. Lizard forks 1–100 copies and pauses the source briefly. E2B pauses the source, captures it, and drops its active connections. Runtime freezes the source while memory is written.

Others fork the disk only. Sandboxer's fork gets a new identity and boots fresh. Agent 37's fork copies the disk while the source keeps running. InstaBox's fork is snapshot-save plus create, which is not instant despite the homepage.

splits.heading: Templates decide what you can carry forward
body: E2B and Blaxel build templates from Dockerfiles; Agent 37 pins Dockerfile-built images by digest. Sandboxer, Boat, boxd, Lizard and InstaBox use snapshots as their image mechanism. Morph has devbox templates that integrate a secrets manager.
A fixed catalogue is the narrowest case: Lizard's templates are platform images, and a custom upload flow is not documented.

watchFor: Whether memory and processes are in the snapshot, and whether the source keeps running.
Whether a restore is in place and destructive, or creates a separate machine.
Whether you can choose an older snapshot; Boat cannot.
Whether snapshots contain credentials; InstaBox's include saved logins.
Whether a fork inherits the source's TTL; Boat's and Sandboxer's do not.

rows.note: No snapshot product. Free nightly backups of /home/node with seven restore points, restored in place only; a live fork copies the disk but not memory; templates are Dockerfile-built images.

source.quote: Every instance's data (`/home/node`) is backed up nightly into seven rotating slots

rows.note: A snapshot captures filesystem, running processes and memory, and outlives the sandbox, but it is in private preview and not recommended for production. Fork runs from the snapshot.

source.quote: A snapshot captures the state of a sandbox at a point in time: its filesystem, its running processes, and its memory.

rows.note: Snapshots are automatic, disk-only and taken every minute, but only the newest is usable: there is no point-in-time restore. Saved snapshots are named and never expire.

source.quote: Resume and fork always use the newest snapshot. You cannot go back to an older one.

rows.note: A snapshot keeps memory and disk, is named and versioned, and boots machines already running; a checkpoint is an in-place undo point; backups are disk-only and off-cluster; a fork copies memory and disk in 100–200 ms.

source.quote: A snapshot is a saved copy of a specific machine. It captures the disk and the memory

rows.note: Snapshots capture filesystem and memory while the source keeps running, and filesystem-only snapshots are available. Up to 20 forks from a running VM, with a brief pause and dropped connections.

source.quote: Snapshots let you create a persistent point-in-time capture of a running sandbox, including both its filesystem and memory state.

rows.note: Snapshots are disk-only and may stop the machine to take them; a fork is snapshot-save plus create, not an instant clone; snapshots survive deleting the machine and include saved logins.

source.quote: It is snapshot save plus create, so it takes about as long as those two.

rows.note: A snapshot captures memory, processes and the whole disk and restores into a new sandbox at the source's size; a fork copies a running sandbox 1–100 times with memory, pausing the source briefly.

source.quote: A snapshot saves a running sandbox's memory, running processes and every file on its disk.

rows.note: Snapshots are immutable copies of memory and disk; a branch creates several running instances from one snapshot. Starting a snapshot restores memory, while booting it is a cold boot.

source.quote: Snapshots are immutable point-in-time copies of both memory and disk state.

rows.note: Snapshots default to memory plus disk, with disk-only opt-in; forks copy files, memory and processes but freeze the source while capturing; a sandbox with a volume cannot be snapshotted.

source.quote: Snapshots default to `mode: "memory"`. That mode keeps files, memory and running processes.

rows.note: Three snapshot kinds: a stop snapshot with disk and memory, continuous disk snapshots every ten minutes, and named disk snapshots used as templates with share codes. Forks are disk-only.

source.quote: Every 10 minutes while a sandbox runs, and at every stop

rows.note: Checkpoints snapshot the writable filesystem, copy-on-write and without interrupting work; they restore in place and overwrite current files. A live fork or create-from-checkpoint is not documented.

source.quote: A checkpoint snapshots the writable filesystem overlay: everything you've added on top of the base image.

rows.note: Snapshots capture the filesystem and outlive the sandbox; taking one manually stops the session. Fork uses the current snapshot or falls back to a fresh create from the image.

source.quote: You can also snapshot a running sandbox at any time by calling `snapshot()`, which captures its current filesystem before stopping the session.
